title: How America hijacked Western philosophy
subtitle: Richard Rorty and the reinvention of Pragmatism
author: Steve Fuller
introduction: America has long been seen as a latecomer to philosophy, trying to play catch-up with Europe. But according to philosopher Steve Fuller, this misreads what pragmatists like James, Dewey, and Rorty were up to. The American Pragmatists weren’t joining the existing Western philosophical tradition. They were hijacking it, recasting truth, meaning, and reason in terms that placed America at the center of history.
body:
Richard Rorty was the greatest Pragmatist philosopher of the second half of the twentieth century. He didn’t have much competition. Pragmatism had effectively died with John Dewey in 1952, if not earlier. Before Rorty burst on the US philosophical scene in the 1970s, self-described “Pragmatists” were usually teaching the history of philosophy, as Rorty himself was at Princeton. By the lights of the dominant analytic school of philosophy (both then and now), history is a low-rent district. However, if the low-rent district is located in America’s premier philosophy department, ideas coming from there could have impact, a prospect that Rorty fully exploited.

Rorty sometimes called his philosophy “Neo-Pragmatism,” but it was really a reinvention of the original movement, a “Pragmatism 2.0.” Rorty had the advantage of living after Pragmatism 1.0 had run its course, which allowed him to see it in what Kant would regard as “aesthetic” terms. In the Critique of Judgement, Kant famously said that art is purposive while lacking a purpose. We might now say that art is meaningful even if we don’t know the exact meaning—or even if such a meaning is to be known. The same applies to philosophical movements. In Pragmatism’s heyday, philosophers argued about whether its reduction of meaning and truth to instrumental value did sufficient justice to these hallowed concepts. But once that discursive moment had passed, the question remained, “What was that (Pragmatism) all about?” Rorty’s “Neo-Pragmatism” was an answer to that question.

Pragmatism’s doctrines had precedents in what was then the recent history of European philosophy, especially Kant’s association of “practical reason” with will power and Mill’s expansive conception of utility to include all human value. Its elevation of these moral theories into a general worldview reached back to medieval nominalism’s attitudes towards language and truth. But above all, Pragmatism came from the United States of America, a newcomer to the philosophical conversation that was taken seriously by its European interlocutors, even as they disagreed with what the likes of William James and John Dewey were propounding. In our decidedly “postcolonial” times, the introduction of such non-European voices was notable, since it started a generation before the balance of global power had begun to shift decisively across the Atlantic.

Before he died in 1830, Hegel had predicted (prophesied?) that the United States was the next landing zone for the world-historic spirit.

And while it was fashionable for virtually all twentieth-century schools of philosophy to blame Hegel for everything wrong with the field, he can be reasonably credited with inspiring the nascent American philosophical community to assert itself on the world stage. Hegel famously proposed that the world-historic spirit, like the sun, rose in the East and set in the West, perhaps to rise again. (China now banks on that.) Before he died in 1830, Hegel had predicted (prophesied?) that the United States was the next landing zone for the world-historic spirit.

Moreover, Hegel wasn’t simply suffering from an overextended metaphor. German immigration to the US in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries was considerable and impactful in ways that have yet to be given their full due. German Idealism dominated American philosophy departments long after it had ceased to bear fruit in its native soil. Indeed, Dewey is arguably seen as a “recovering Hegelian.” One of James’ Harvard colleagues, Josiah Royce, wrote the first history of his native California in 1886, long before Hollywood, the aerospace industry, and Silicon Valley. It created the Hegelian impression that California, as the most westward state, was the future of both America and the world—a vision that dominated the twentieth-century imaginary.

An important feature of the Hegelian narrative is that the scene of world-historic action shifts in both time and space. It is not “organic” in the classical sense of something evolving in the same place over time. It is more like relay racing, in which one nation passes the baton to the next to complete the race. This means that each nation must wait its turn, so to speak, during which they observe their predecessors in action. In this respect, one initially enters what Rorty, adapting a phrase of Michael Oakeshott’s, called “the conversation of mankind” as an eavesdropper and only gradually becomes a full-fledged interlocutor, often after the overheard conversants have left the stage.

This is not as strange as it first sounds. The idea that philosophers literally respond to each other’s arguments is arguably only enforced in analytic philosophy journals. Normally, even when the philosophers personally know each other, their “communication” consists in each party conjuring up a version of the other which allows them to have the conversation they want to have, even if it involves systematically misreading what the other party is trying to say. Harold Bloom would call it “misprision.” Nevertheless, key to the romance of the history of philosophy has been imagining that the likes of, say, Plato and Hume are indeed exchanging views on topics of common interest, such as “the true” and “the good.” In that respect, as Rorty rightly but politely observed, philosophy is a genre of literary fiction. But that doesn’t make the conversation metaphor any less illuminating.

The inevitable delay in new voices entering “the conversation of mankind” enables the later parties to perceive both needlessly amplified differences among current interlocutors and missed opportunities for taking the conversation in a different, potentially more productive direction. I have characterized the eavesdropper’s semi-detached standpoint to the conversation as “orthogonal,” which literally means “at right angles” to the line of communication. It permits a more balanced approach to discursive antagonists, resulting in blended positions that, at first glance, might appear ambiguous or vague, but which are better seen in the spirit of a Hegelian dialectical synthesis. Rorty’s characteristically deflationary way of putting this radical shift in standpoint can be summed up as, “Ask not what philosophy can teach America but what America can learn from philosophy.”

SUGGESTED READING After metaphysics: Rorty and American Pragmatism By Elin Danielsen Huckerby

A good example is William James’ original 1907 formulation of Pragmatism as a theory of “meaning” and “truth” in the broad sense of both terms, which initially struck many European philosophers as “pre-philosophical,” since they had been following Kant’s lead in drawing a sharp distinction between epistemology and ethics. And even within ethics, it had already become customary to follow John Stuart Mill in contrasting Kant’s intention-based and Bentham’s consequence-based justification for moral action. However, Pragmatism came at these matters from a different angle, one that either “confused” or “transcended” these distinctions. Its signature move was to return the mental faculty of the will to the heart of philosophical discourse.

The will historically carried religious connotations reaching back to St Augustine’s discussion of humanity’s original disobedience of God. James’ thorough secularization involved equating the will with the tenacity to follow through on one’s ideas, something that psychology can experimentally study in terms of attention and focus. Indeed, perhaps James’ most famous public lecture, “The Will to Believe,” came close to arguing that to believe something is to act as if it were true, in the sense of “where there’s a will, there’s a way.” That sensibility, widely seen as emblematic of America’s “frontier spirit,” confounded Europeans who insisted on neat distinctions between epistemology and ethics, intention and consequence.

To be sure, will-centered philosophies were well known in late nineteenth and early twentieth-century Europe. But they were usually seen as offering a pessimistic, destructive, if not outright nihilistic vision, either of oneself (in the case of Schopenhauer) or the entire social order (in the case of Nietzsche). In that respect, memory of humanity’s biblical insubordination lingered in the minds of these avowed atheists. In contrast, Pragmatism proposed a much more positive, even uplifting vision of humanity as creating the world as it goes along, responding to the obstacles that it faced along the way. We are good and can get better.

In his later work, Rorty discussed this blended optimism under the rubric of “hope,” which he offered as a replacement for the epistemic and ethical attitudes normally discussed in academic philosophy. Moreover, he increasingly leaned into American history, offering it as a model of hope in action, without proposing a formula for generating hope, let alone for reproducing the US experience of hope across the world. Rorty’s care not to universalize his perspective had less to do with any commitment to relativism than with a vision of philosophy as a field that projects the future as an open space of possibilities for others to pursue in their own directions. Hegel would have been pleased.

Philosophy is a genre of literary fiction.

Finally, it is instructive to observe the shifts in the flow of philosophical conversation in the roughly half-century separating the heyday of Pragmatism and Rorty’s resurrection of the movement. The most obvious one was the migration of European philosophical talent to the United States in response to the rise of Nazism, which helped turn the US into the global philosophical powerhouse of the second half of the twentieth century. However, these émigré philosophers did not adopt Pragmatism to blend into their new environment. On the contrary, the Pragmatists adjusted their philosophy to make it hospitable to the newcomers, arguably abandoning its own distinctiveness in the process, something of which Rorty was acutely aware.

Consider two examples coming from opposite sides of the contemporary philosophical spectrum. On the analytic side, in the 1930s, Harvard philosophy chair and student of James and Royce, C.I. Lewis, commissioned the publication of the collected papers of Charles Sanders Peirce, the mathematically trained polymath now credited as the founder of Pragmatism. Peirce was a friend of James, a teacher of Dewey, but otherwise a reprobate who published disparate essays but no books. However, the collected works seized the interest of Bertrand Russell, who proclaimed Peirce the greatest American logician. On the continental side, Richard Bernstein, a Dewey scholar and classmate of Rorty’s, spent much of his early career repurposing Pragmatism into a “big tent” pluralism that promoted phenomenology, hermeneutics, and Existentialism at a time—the 1960s and ’70s—when the analytic school looked set to take over American academic philosophy. He is now seen as one of the early mentors of Nancy Fraser, Seyla Benhabib, and Judith Butler.

While Rorty regarded both moves as honorable, they did only half the Hegelian job of taking the conversation of mankind forward. They turned Pragmatism into a vessel for receiving the earlier conversants but failed to place Pragmatism’s distinctive stamp on the result. Rorty’s own remedy took inspiration from early twentieth-century US Progressivism, which envisaged America as a “melting pot” of Europe’s displaced peoples, capable of producing a superior human. All the original Pragmatists signed up to this ideology, which Rorty attempted to exemplify in his own practice as a philosopher, fully understanding that eventually—perhaps soon now—the baton will be passed.

This topic is treated in more detail in Steve Fuller's recent book, To Judge and To Justify: Profiles of the Academic Vocation (Springer).
